label: Latin and Catalan
en: There follows another song, for a round dance:
Star shining on the mountain like a sunbeam, on the saw-toothed mountain of miracles, hear the people.
All the peoples run together rejoicing,
rich and poor, great and small;
they climb it so that their eyes may see,
and return from it filled with graces.
Princes and magnates of royal stock,
the powers of the age, having obtained pardon,
confess their sins, beating their breasts,
and on bended knee cry here: Ave Maria.
Prelates and barons, famous counts,
all the religious and the priests,
soldiers, merchants, citizens, sailors,
townsmen, fishermen, are rewarded there.
Peasants, ploughmen, and also notaries,
advocates, sculptors, all the wood-
workers, tailors and cobblers, and also wool-workers,
craftsmen and all give thanks there.
For a round dance:
Queen of all the heavens, our morning star, blot out our sins.
Before the birth a virgin, pregnant by God, you remained ever inviolate.
And in the birth a virgin, fruitful by God, you remained ever inviolate.
And after the birth a virgin, a mother delivered, you remained ever inviolate.
For a round dance:
Let us all sing together: Ave Maria.
While the Virgin was alone, behold, an angel came; he is called Gabriel and was sent from heaven.
With bright face he said: Ave Maria. With bright face he said: hear, dearest ones.
Behold, you shall conceive, Mary, and bear a son, hear, dearest ones; you shall call him Jesus.
Song of the joys of Our Lady in the Catalan vernacular, for a round dance:
We shall recount the seven joys, and singing devoutly
we shall humbly greet the sweet Virgin Mary.
Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you, serene Virgin.
notes: Four of the manuscript's ten songs: the first stanzas of Stella splendens, and Polorum regina, Cuncti simus concanentes and the opening of Los set gotxs, the one in Catalan. Each opens with the manuscript's rubric, telling how it is to be danced (a ball redon, ad trepudium rotundum: as a round dance).

Stella splendens: the "saw-toothed" mountain (serratus) is a play on the name Montserrat, the "sawn mountain"; the song lists pilgrims of every rank, which is why it is often read as a picture of medieval society.
Stella splendens, line 5.2: the source breaks "ligni fabri" (wood-workers, carpenters) across two lines, and the English follows.
The manuscript says these songs were written so that pilgrims keeping vigil in the church could sing and dance decently, since they would sing and dance anyway.
